messages.body_plain:
Hi -- apologies, I'm on parental leave (just had a baby!)... but briefly...

On Tuesday, July 31, 2018 at 3:44:47 AM UTC+12, lizmil...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear Dr. Matzke,
>
> I am preparing to set up a BioGeoBEARS analysis on a very large phylogeny of ~12,000 species. I am interested in transitions among freshwater realms across the whole tree, even though the overall clade also contains many marine species. I have six freshwater areas of interest, and a 7th area that is "restricted to marine", meaning absence from the first six areas. At least half of the species in this phylogeny belong to the "marine" category. Marine and freshwater categories show reasonably strong conservatism, with some subclades having no transitions among realms, and some having many transitions. My interest is in the timing and frequency of transitions among freshwater areas, say Neotropics and Afrotropics. Marine groups represent one possible intermediate transition between freshwater realms, and are not otherwise of interest in my study.
>
> Since the starting phylogeny is so large, I am exploring options to cut down tips in the "marine" category to save on computation time. I have thought of three options, though you may have other suggestions: (1) Keep phylogeny as-is, with ~6,000 tips coded as "marine". (2) Trim marine clades down to only 1 tip per clade, unless they have freshwater species nested within them. (3) Only analyze separate subclades in the phylogeny that are predominately freshwater, then combine results later on.
>
> I am worried about how the latter two approaches may bias my results. Would you expect the trimming described above to dramatically change the inferred transition timing in other clades? Do you have any other concerns I haven't thought of?

So...no solution is perfect or unbiased here. All the biogeography models here are in effect assuming a Yule process for the phylogeny (pure-birth, no lineage extinction, no unsampled species).  It would be very rare to have those assumptions met.  The simulations in Matzke (2014) suggest that for a basic question like ancestral range probabilities or DEC/DEC+J comparisons, random extinction/missing taxa increase uncertainty a bit but don't bias results. Area-specific biases in extinction sampling would have a much higher chance of biasing results -- e.g. if everything in Antarctica is extinct, you won't be able to reconstruct Antarctica as an ancestral range, even if it was in real life (e.g. for marsupials), unless additional constraints are put into the analysis.

Reducing "marine" clades down to a single tip is very much like imposing an area-specific extinction even that reduces, say, a diverse clade from South America down to a single species.

Re: computation time, this should just be linear with the number of tips, e.g. 12000 taxa will only take twice as long as 6000 taxa. In the world of computational time, this is a small difference.

Much more important would be the size of the state space, e.g.

6 areas/realms = 2^6 ranges = 64 states in the state space
7 areas/realms = 2^7 ranges = 128 states in the state space

...so, 7 areas will be more than twice as slow as 6 areas (something like 4 times slower I think).  If you set maxareas = 2, though, this decreases a lot:

numstates_from_numareas(6,2)
[1] 21
numstates_from_numareas(7,2)
[1] 28

...so it depends on whether you have a lot of species occupying multiple realms or not.

See this on state spaces:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#how_geog_areas

The bigger potential "bias" is that, if half the species are marine, and "marine" is one realm, this will be a lot of signal for realm conservatism, and because the models assume the same parameters work across the whole tree, this would somewhat "bias" the estimate of the j parameter: more conservatism would mean lower j.  I put "bias" in quotes because it's simply a function of the data -- if half the data show no change, any parameters estimating the probability of change will be lower.

One way around this would be to use a manual dispersal multiplier matrix to make there be a 0.1 multiplier difference between marine-nonmarine transitions, and within-nonmarine transitions (multiplier 1.0). Then make the "w" parameter free and estimate it.  0.1^w will be the estimated multiplier on transitions for between marine-nonmarine events. See Dupin, Matzke et al. 2017, J Biogeog for the basic idea.

Option (3) would be another method, but is a bit more complex, and disallows inference of the marine-nonmarine transitions, which might be interesting (and interesting to compare to within-nonmarine transitions).  You could:

- run a bunch of individual separate clades and just compare the parameters etc. -- a rough way of dealing with heterogeneity between clades

- or you could assume homogeneity across all clades and infer the parameters once for all clades at once. This would be a bit of a custom scripting job to set up though.

If it were me, I would run the full tree, and attempt to use the +w, +x etc. model variants to learn parameters to test hypotheses about causes of transitions -- e.g., perhaps marine-brackish transitions are easier than marine-freshwater stream transitions (for instance).

Additional things can be imagined with such a big dataset, e.g. estimating all the different possible transition rates as separate parameters, but things like this would be a biggish custom job to set up (email me if interested).

Cheers, Nick

>
> Thank you for your help!
> Best,
> Liz Miller

messages.subject: Problem with dispersal matricies
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm having huge trouble getting BioGeoBears to understand my dispersal matricies file. I've re-written it multiple times and it's driving me a bit crazy so I'm hoping someone here can help. I've looked through other people's example files and others' problems and tried to fix everything I can see that's wrong but I still keep getting error messages. When I try to load the dispersal matricies using:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object = readfiles_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)

I get 35 warnings. These 35 warnings are all:

In read_dispersal_multipliers_fn(inputs) : NAs introduced by coercion

I have 36 dispersal matricies so I assume it is the same problem for all my dispersal matricies. If I ignore these warnings and go ahead to setting up the DEC model, when I check for error using:

check_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)

I get the following:

Error in inputs$list_of_dispersal_multipliers_mats[[1]] :
  subscript out of bounds

This is the first time I've tried to use BioGeoBears so please forgive my ignorance. Also, I'd appreciate answers in English, not R, or binary, as I'm also by no means and R expert...!!

The dispersal matrix file is attached.

Many thanks in advance,

Susie

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am trying to run an DEC+J analysis on a big dataset (360 terminals and 10 Areas).

All the input files are working fine, and the check_BioGeoBEARS_run() say it is a go.

Once  I get the run going, after a while R returns the following message to me:

Error: vector memory exhausted (limit reached?)

Is this due to my computer or due to the run setup?

This is the script I am using:

setwd("~/")
source("scripts/biogeobears-utilities.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")
require(parallel)
require(FD)
require(snow)
require(minqa)
load.biogeobears()

calc_loglike_sp = compiler::cmpfun(calc_loglike_sp_prebyte)
calc_independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch = compiler::cmpfun(calc_independent_likelihoods_on_each_branch_prebyte)

decj.potamo <- define_BioGeoBEARS_run()

phylo.path <- "data/potamo_ultra.newick"
moref(phylo.path)
potamo.tree <- read.tree(phylo.path)

# uncomment if needed
# plot(potamo.tree)
# prt(potamo.tree, get_tipnames = T)

decj.potamo$trfn = "data/potamo_ultra.newick"
decj.potamo$trfn #check if correctly assigned

geo.path <- "data/potamo_code_geog.data"
moref(geo.path)
getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP(lgdata_fn=geo.path) #infer ranges from phylip file

decj.potamo$geogfn = "data/potamo_code_geog.data"
decj.potamo$geogfn #check if correclty assigned

decj.potamo = configure.standard.biogeobears.run(decj.potamo)

decj.potamo$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","type"] = "free"
decj.potamo$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","init"] = 0.0001
decj.potamo$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","est"] = 0.0001
decj.potamo$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"] = 0.0001

decj.potamo$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

decj.potamo$return_condlikes_table = T
decj.potamo$calc_TTL_loglike_from_condlikes_table = T
decj.potamo$calc_ancprobs = T

check_BioGeoBEARS_run(decj.potamo)
decj.potamo

decj.results = bears_optim_run(decj.potamo)
save(decj.results, file="results/decj.potamo.Rdata")

If needed, I can provide the tree file and the area data

Cheers

JP

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- this is the second time this morning someone has mentioned an error like this, I wonder if they changed something in R recently that lowers the default memory allocation.  10 areas and 360 tips has never been a problem before...

(the issue, probably, is that for parallel processing of the matrix exponentations, BioGeoBEARS sets up an array of size numstates x numstates x numbranches, this would be 1024x1024x359 for you, so it can get big)

Short term solution is probably to set the number of cores to use to 1, or google how to increase R's memory allocation.

Cheers,
Nick

If your goal was to get a nice table of the range probabilities for each node, see:

Table of probabilities of states/ranges at each node

Nick

> 1. Is there anyway I can export the results (result.obj), more precisely the plot, in a newick annotated format?

There is no code currently that does this. I imagine it would be a semi-major project.

But, all of the BioGeoBEARS plots are generated using basic APE graphics functions -- look at the code inside plot_BioGeoBEARS_results().

All you need to do your own plots with basic APE plot.phylo() are:

1. The tree
2. The table with range probabilities per node
3. An understanding of how the node numbers work for trees in R

1. The tree you have.

2. For the table, see:
Table of probabilities of states/ranges at each node
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#node_probabilities

3. For understanding the node numbers, see the prt() function (prints tree to a data.frame table)

>
> 2. Between each one of the ancestral nodes, there is an "elbow", or "corner", that also receive a state "tag". I have attached to this email one figure detail of this "elbow". Can it also be removed from the plot?

Yes, I call them "corners".  They represent the ranges "instantaneously" after speciation. They can be removed from the plot by setting

plotsplits=FALSE

in the plot_BioGeoBEARS_results() function.

Cheers!
Nick
